clue.text: Ray must keep right, Ray must keep right, Ray must keep right …?

definitions.text: Ray must keep right, Ray must keep right, Ray must keep right …?

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so one piece holds the other inside

parts.note: a manta is a large species of ray
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone drilling a rule of the road into a driver called Ray, over and over.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'Ray must keep right' is the wordplay, MANT(R)A; the whole clue, a phrase chanted again and again, then illustrates the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A mantra is a word or phrase repeated over and over, as in meditation or as a slogan, which the repeated line demonstrates.

clue.text: Indian city's river in range

indicators.note: being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: an Aga is a make of range cooker
R is the usual abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A geography note about a river running through a mountain range near an Indian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Range' suggests mountains, but here it is a kitchen range; an Aga is a traditional heavy cast-iron cooker common in British country kitchens.
explanation.definitionFit: Agra is a city in Uttar Pradesh, northern India, home of the Taj Mahal.

clue.text: Sick and worried after idiot shows interest

parts.note: tit is British slang for a fool
sick means unwell
as in 'what's eating you?', to eat is to worry

explanation.surface: Someone feeling sick and anxious after a fool turns up and takes an interest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the idiot first, then sick and worried in order. 'Shows' is a link: the wordplay shows the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To titillate is to arouse pleasurable excitement or curiosity, a stronger form of the verb 'interest'.

clue.text: I see stuff about Sabbath in hermitage perhaps

indicators.note: to be about something is to be around it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: 'Ah' is what you say when you see the point
S is an abbreviation for Sabbath
to ram is to stuff or cram in

explanation.surface: A hermit reflecting on the religious things surrounding the Sabbath in a retreat.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation goes around S, and the verb 'stuff' follows. 'Perhaps' marks the definition as an example rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An ashram is a secluded religious retreat in India, a kind of hermitage where devotees live and meditate.

clue.text: Model deep in trouble checks how to change name

indicators.note: to check is to restrain or hold back, so one piece holds the other in

parts.note: a doll is a model of a person

indicators.note: things in trouble are thrown into disorder, so the letters get jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A fashion model in deep trouble looks into how to change her name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like the troubled person, but it is the outer piece, and the scrambled word sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A deed poll is the British legal document a person signs to change their name officially.

clue.text: Engineer scheduled items about a scourge of the countryside

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so the rearranged letters go around
to engineer is to contrive or rework, so these letters are rebuilt in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged
taken as written

explanation.surface: A planner arranging an agenda of items about a rural menace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' reads as a noun, a person, but works as a verb on the two words that follow; the single A goes inside the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Dutch elm disease is a fungal blight that killed most of Britain's elm trees from the 1960s, a plague on rural landscapes.

clue.text: Space in the middle of stable

parts.note: an en is a printer's space
during means in the course or middle of

explanation.surface: Room in the centre of a horse's stable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stable' looks like a noun for horses, but it is the adjective meaning steady. An en is a typesetting space half an em wide.
explanation.definitionFit: Something enduring lasts and stays firm over time, which is a sense of stable as an adjective.

clue.text: Almost clear communion plate

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is cut

parts.note: patent means obvious or clear

explanation.surface: A communion plate that has been nearly cleared of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clear' is the adjective, as in patently obvious, not the verb to clear a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A paten is the small dish, usually silver or gold, that holds the bread during the Eucharist.

clue.text: Infatuated voter lucks out

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or awry, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A smitten voter has no luck at the ballot box.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lucks out' is an idiom for getting lucky, which hides that 'out' is the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Being lovestruck means being overwhelmed by romantic feeling, the same state as infatuation.

clue.text: Note linked loops? About time!

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece goes round the other

parts.note: crochet is needlework made of interlinked loops of yarn
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An exasperated note that the knitting has finally been finished: about time!
explanation.walkthrough: 'About time!' looks like an exclamation of impatience, but splits into the container signal and a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a crotchet is the musical note lasting one beat, the American quarter note.

clue.text: Director rejected musical, in case

parts.note: D is an abbreviation for director

indicators.note: rejected means sent back, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: Evita is the Lloyd Webber musical about Eva Perón

explanation.surface: A stage director turning down a musical just in case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In case' reads as 'as a precaution', but 'case' is grammar and 'in' only joins it to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The dative is a grammatical case, used in Latin and German for the indirect object of a verb.

clue.text: Hardened nature of Great Russian leader initially leaving wearing not so much

indicators.note: whoever wears clothes sits inside them, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: less means not so much

indicators.note: the first letter leaves, so the opening letter is removed

parts.note: Catherine the Great was Empress of Russia

explanation.surface: A tough Russian ruler departs dressed in very little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great' looks like an adjective, but it belongs to the leader's title; with her C gone, she is worn inside the other word.
explanation.definitionFit: Leatheriness is the quality of being tough and hard like leather, so a hardened nature or texture.

clue.text: Glamorous woman in pub to attempt to tour earth on endless jolly

indicators.note: with no ends, the first and last letters are removed

parts.note: a bar is a pub

indicators.note: touring means going round, so one piece travels around another

parts.note: a bid is an attempt
E is the abbreviation for earth
the word with both ends lost

explanation.surface: A glamorous woman in a pub plans a round-the-world jolly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jolly' looks like an outing, and also tempts as an adjective; here it just loses both outer letters. 'On' puts that piece after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A Barbie doll is slang for a conventionally pretty, groomed woman, after the famous toy figure.

clue.text: A prisoner returned for festivity

indicators.note: returned means sent back the way it came, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: taken as written
a lag is a convict, usually an old lag

explanation.surface: A prisoner comes back home in time for a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' is British slang for a convict, especially a long-serving one.
explanation.definitionFit: A gala is a festive occasion or celebration, often with entertainment, so a synonym for festivity.

clue.text: Prominent feature of songbird going round with male

indicators.note: to go round something is to encircle it, so one piece encloses the rest

parts.note: the lark is a songbird
and means with or plus
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: The most noticeable thing about a singing bird is its circling with a mate.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird encloses the other two short pieces, in the order they appear.
explanation.definitionFit: A landmark is an easily seen object or feature of a landscape, standing out from its surroundings.

clue.text: Regularly bump heavies off, and cause trouble

indicators.note: off means gone wrong, so these letters are disordered
at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: its first and third letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Thugs who routinely kill people off and stir up trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bump off' reads as gangster slang for murder, but the words split: 'off' rearranges the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: To misbehave is to act badly or make mischief, so to cause trouble.

clue.text: Former England cricket captain's heart fluttering before century

indicators.note: fluttering things flap about irregularly, so the letters move around

parts.note: taken as written
a ton is a hundred, as in a century of runs

explanation.surface: A former captain's nerves flutter as he nears a hundred runs.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Atherton captained England's cricket team in the 1990s. 'Century' is cricket for a hundred runs, giving ton.
explanation.definitionFit: Mike Atherton led the England Test side in more matches than almost anyone, between 1993 and 2001.

clue.text: Editor backing item demurred

indicators.note: to back something is to stand behind it, so this piece comes after the other

parts.note: an object is a thing or item
ED is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: An editor supporting a news item had doubts about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' sounds like support, or a reversal, but in a across answer it means coming behind: the editor sits at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: To demur is to raise an objection or show reluctance, so objected is a past-tense synonym.

clue.text: Fed up of criticism having no point, ultimately

indicators.note: having none of something means it is taken out

parts.note: stick is informal for criticism, as in 'took a lot of stick'

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: its final letter

explanation.surface: Tired of pointless criticism, in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' in British English means harsh criticism. 'Fed up of' is a common British variant of 'fed up with'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sick of something means being weary and annoyed by it, which is exactly fed up.

clue.text: Relish cream with lardy-cake on vacation

parts.note: the cream or pick is the best of a group

indicators.note: vacating means emptying out, so only the outer letters stay

parts.note: its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Enjoying cream with a rich cake while on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relish' looks like a verb meaning enjoy, but it is the noun for a condiment. Lardy cake is a rich English bread cake made with lard.
explanation.definitionFit: A pickle is a chutney-like condiment of preserved vegetables, so a type of relish.

clue.text: Go and wish happiness to recruit in part of Scotland

parts.note: to go is a euphemism for to urinate
to bless is to wish someone well
to hire is to take on staff

explanation.surface: Travelling to congratulate a new recruit somewhere in Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go' means travel in the surface but is the toilet euphemism in the wordplay. Peeblesshire is a former county in the Scottish Borders.
explanation.definitionFit: Peeblesshire is a historic county in southern Scotland, around the town of Peebles.

clue.text: Primarily, Brits hate any jalapenos in fried vegetables

definitions.note: the answer is singular; a bhaji is a fritter made of several vegetables

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letters are taken

parts.note: opening letters of these four words
its opening letter

explanation.surface: British diners mostly dislike hot peppers in their fried snacks.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letters run through 'in', which is also the link; a bhaji is a staple of British Indian restaurants.
explanation.definitionFit: An onion bhaji is a spiced Indian fritter of vegetables deep-fried in gram-flour batter.

clue.text: Helpers claimed to be cycling

indicators.note: cycling means going round, so the letter at one end moves to the other

parts.note: said means claimed or stated

explanation.surface: Assistants reported to be riding bicycles.
explanation.walkthrough: The first letter moves round to the end of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Aids are things or people that help, such as teaching aids or hearing aids, so helpers.

clue.text: Spooner's encouragement for Homer's son, an actor

indicators.note: Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds are exchanged

parts.note: Bart is Homer Simpson's son, and 'go' cheers him on

explanation.surface: Cheering on a Simpsons character in an actor's voice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Homer' suggests the Greek poet, but it is Homer Simpson; swapping the G and B sounds gives the film star's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Humphrey Bogart was the Hollywood star of Casablanca and The Maltese Falcon, so an actor.

clue.text: American bishop can start to address disputed region in Georgia

parts.note: A is an abbreviation for American
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
khazi is British slang for a toilet, as is can

indicators.note: a start is a beginning, so only the first letter is used

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: A US bishop may begin speaking about a contested territory in the Caucasus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like a verb, but it is American slang for a toilet, matched by khazi, its British slang equivalent. 'Georgia' is the country, not the US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Abkhazia is a breakaway region of the country Georgia whose independence is recognised by only a few states.

clue.text: Everybody in church welcomes a marriage

parts.note: all means everybody

indicators.note: to welcome is to take in, so one piece holds another

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: The whole congregation turns out to greet a wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like a link placing everybody in church, but it is a piece of the answer that takes in the A.
explanation.definitionFit: An alliance is a union or bond, and a marriage is a union of two people or families.

clue.text: Still love following proceedings when temperature's dropped

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this piece is placed at the end
something dropped is let go, so a letter is removed

parts.note: events are proceedings or happenings
T is the abbreviation for temperature
love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: Still in love after events, even when the weather cools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' places the love after the proceedings, once T has been taken out of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Still, used as an adverb, means nevertheless, which is what the phrase even so means.
